title: Pour-Over Coffee Starter Kit: Everything You Need
excerpt: A dripper, filters and a gooseneck kettle: the three pieces you need to start brewing café-style pour-over at home.

body.p: Pour-over coffee is clean, bright and easy to fine-tune, and the gear is cheaper than most coffee makers. You need three things: a dripper, the right paper filters and a kettle that pours slowly. Add a burr grinder and you have the same setup many specialty cafés use.

The V60 is the most popular pour-over cone in the world for good reason. Its spiral ridges and single large hole let the speed of your pour control the brew. Pour slowly for a stronger cup or faster for a lighter one. The ceramic version is made in Japan from traditional Arita-yaki porcelain and holds heat well. Size 02 makes one to four cups.
Just starting out, or want one for travel? The plastic V60 brews the same way, weighs almost nothing and won't break.

V60 cones need V60-shaped filters. Regular flat-bottom filters won't fit. Buy the size that matches your dripper (02 for both drippers above), and rinse each filter with hot water before adding coffee so it doesn't add a papery taste.

body.h: 3. The kettle: why a gooseneck matters

body.p: A regular kettle dumps water in a splash. A gooseneck spout lets you pour a thin, steady stream exactly where you want it, which is the whole trick of pour-over. The Cosori is our pick because it adds temperature control, with five presets and a 60-minute keep-warm, so you can hit about 200°F every time.

If you just want the gooseneck pour without the extra features, the Chefman is a simple one-switch kettle with fast boiling and boil-dry protection. Let it rest about 30 seconds after boiling before you pour.

ul: 15 g coffee (about 2.5 tablespoons), ground medium-fine, to 250 g water (about 8.5 oz).
Rinse the filter, add the coffee and level the bed.
Bloom: pour about 30 g of water, just enough to wet the grounds, and wait 30–45 seconds.
Pour the rest in slow circles over 1.5 minutes, avoiding the filter walls.
Total brew time should be about 3 minutes. Too slow means grind coarser. Too fast means grind finer.

body.p: Grind size makes or breaks pour-over. If you don't own a burr grinder yet, start with our guide to the best burr coffee grinders.
